This requested counterexample cannot be supplied, because its existence would refute the **Jacobian conjecture** (Keller, 1939), which is open in characteristic 0 for every dimension \(d\ge 2\).

Concretely, for a polynomial map \(F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3\):
- \(\det J_F\in\mathbb C^\times\) “constant” means the Jacobian determinant is a *unit* of the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,x_3]\), i.e. a nonzero scalar.
- The implication “\(\det J_F\) constant nonzero \(\Rightarrow\) \(F\) injective \(\Rightarrow\) \(F\) a polynomial automorphism” is exactly the Jacobian conjecture.
- A pair of distinct exact points \(p\neq q\) with \(F(p)=F(q)\) while \(\det J_F\) is a nonzero constant would therefore be a genuine disproof of a major open problem. No such example is known (over \(\mathbb C\), over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), or over any number field, since polynomial identities and collisions there extend to \(\mathbb C\)).

The only known counterexamples to a “real Jacobian” statement (e.g. Pinchuk’s map \(\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\)) have a Jacobian determinant that is everywhere nonzero **but not constant**; when viewed over \(\mathbb C\) it acquires zeros, so it is not a unit of \(\mathbb C[x,y]\). Hence it does not satisfy the hypothesis here.
